utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And there was no need for that. I can explain, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If necessary, we will ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go through the documents that the Prosecution showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to have document P1044 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document, if you see under Roman I, the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior adopted on the 5th of April, 1996, is mentioned, and I think yesterday you testified on that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The rules shown to you by the Prosecution were adopted in 1994. Can we agree that the document shown to you -- but now, if we agree that it was brought in 1994, we can agree that this wasn't in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot answer that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not your fault. It was a question by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a fact that all the ministries had to have rules of internal organisation; that is a fact. The rules are adopted by the minister, with the agreement of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 of the document on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to shorten the questions because we've already covered some topics. We see under number 4: "The SMs in charge of border crossing control send information directly to the authorised department in the ministry and the secretariat on whose territory they are located." Can it be seen from these rules that the police stations in charge of state border controls, according to these rules were not duty-bound to inform the MUP staff which existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written in the rules, but in practice it was not like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever work in a SUP that was on -- a border SUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But there was a person in the staff charged with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P1052 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, we have before us a work-plan of the communications station, and my learned friend Mr. Fila put questions to you about that. He asked you about this name "Joint Command" and the Pastrik code. You said you did not know who that indicated.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there were Ibar-40 and Osa-1 codes as well.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are these actually units that are all from the Kosovska Mitrovica territory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which unit is not from the Kosovska Mitrovica area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP 3rd and 4th Detachment were not from the Kosovska Mitrovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But did they stay in that area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that is where they were billeted, in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica. I was saying yesterday that this facility was built inside the barracks compound, and that is where there were members of the PJP there, too, who were engaged on special assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We don't see a date on this document or the place where the actual station was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You cannot see that based on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you cannot tell what the task was for which this strength was formed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not here. But these names - and I said that yesterday during my examination-in-chief - they were used during 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We do have to part of your testimony. In actions for a certain specific area, was a Joint Command formed that would conduct smaller operations and that these would be ad hoc Joint Commands, do you know anything about that, and that this would be the case, such a case here in this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's something that I really have no knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P1072 on e-court, please. Can we now look at the bottom of page 2. This is the rules establishing the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior of SUP Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that this is from January 1994, when this document was enacted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because there is a translation, I'm going to use the Prosecution exhibit. During the proceedings, we are going to provide the version in force, but now I'm going to ask you to tell me what you can. The rules has no number on the first page. It just says "January 1994." And on the last page, even though you cannot see it, it says "/92," as if it were published in 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, you can't see it, but it doesn't really matter. Is it usual for such a document to bear a stamp and signature of the minister if it is an act that is in effect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say until I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this particular document does not contain those things, and you -- did you usually receive copies for use that were uncertified?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last page of each such act should have a number registered, and also it should have a signature and a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is the purpose of using this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is similar to one which is in force -- which was in force at that time. Because I don't have translated the right one, I have to use this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this one wasn't used in examination-in-chief, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was used. And what was the issue drawn from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was just introduced. I don't know what the -- my learned colleague didn't dwell too long on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why don't you wait until the Defence case and use the one in force at the time at that stage? Is there any particular purpose to be achieved by cross-examining on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can -- yeah, I can wait for the Defence case, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, obviously if it needs to be done with this one, fine, but it sounds to me as though it's going to be a waste of time. If you disagree, please say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll skip it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like for P1100 to be placed on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvetic, yesterday you testified about -- or on this exhibit by the Prosecution. I will make use of that opportunity and your knowledge, so as to ask you something pertaining to the document. We can see that a lot of information was entered in this report, which covered only 24 hours. This was information received by the MUP staff from one of the secretariats in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the MUP staff in Kosovo did not have its own personnel to collect information in the field, but they relied exclusively on the information gained from the SUPs. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP staff in Kosovo received information exclusively from the SUPs, but also from its own staff members who were tasked with specific areas as part of their staff work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is all staff personnel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And every assistant of the head of staff was tasked with a specific area, and he followed information from that area and he had his own structure of gaining information. He would address the appropriate person within the SUPs so as to be given information. And the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this is informing, if I may call it, pursuant to the lines of work, the established lines?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From this Prosecution exhibit we can see that during the 24 hours in question there were 24 people killed by terrorists, and there were 31 people injured. It is precisely what you had mentioned, that at the beginning of that year the KLA stepped up its activities. Is it correct that the KLA increased them further come the start of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see on the document the reference to these --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, under number 2, Arabic number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First page, 1, 2, terrorist attacks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, yeah. Because I recollect yesterday that there were references in this document to dates earlier than the 27th of March. But these were all attacks in that 24-hour period, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's how these reports were composed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But -- can we go to the next page of the document, please. You see the references to all these attacks on earlier days?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can clarify it with the witness, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that would help. But that's why I'm asking whether in fact these figures do relate to a limited period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, His Honour Judge Bonomy noticed that this report contains data for a period over 24 hours. Is it correct that this report included information gained in those 24 hours, although it doesn't mean that the incidents mentioned had to take place within the designated time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see some events here dated the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is one concerning the 25th. Perhaps you don't see it at the bottom of the page, an attack by NATO forces on the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can see it. Yes, the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this take place within your SUP as well, that you included events in certain reports which had taken place previously?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were not made part of the previous report, then they were included in the following report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next one is almost invisible, the first part at least in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the next page, thanks. In fact, just before you -- hold on, hold on -- yeah, that's okay now. And the next one. Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you why in the chapter serious crimes committed in this document there is no mention of the murders of civilians in Suva Reka and Podujevo. I wanted to ask you this: Of course you cannot recall the date, but if we know that, for example, the event in Podujevo took place on the 28th of March, 1999, of course it couldn't have been included in the report of the 27th of March, 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The explanation as for why there is no mention of the incident in Suva Reka, could that be because the MUP staff had not been advised on the part of the SUP of Prizren about the event in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one of the assumptions, that they had not been informed, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1114 put on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To add something, if they were not notified on that day and if it was not included in the report of that day, then they should have included it in the report once notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, but if they were not notified at all, it wouldn't appear in any of the reports.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe you have this before you on the screen as well. This is P1114. There is a mention of the reserve police squads, and you've given abundant information on that topic so far. However, I will try to abuse of you further and to gain even more, if possible. Yesterday you said exactly what the number was of the RPO members; it was 1.999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Kosovska Mitrovica territory.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica, the police force, both the active and reserve officers, amounted to 1999 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems I misunderstood. I apologise. What people did the RPOs comprise, which formations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. The reserve police squads, or rather, the concept of their formation existed solely for the purpose of defending villages. In plain terms, in lay terms, one could see that as the arming of villages, but that is not so. It reads reserve police squads to defend villages. Someone even -- some people even used it to show that the Serbs were being armed, but that is incorrect. These are RPOs prescribed by the direction on the performing of tasks, of workers employed in internal affairs issued by the minister of the interior in June 1998 when such RPOs were being formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said yesterday that in reserve police detachments or squads in Kosovska Mitrovica there were a total of 2.000 men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the reserve police squads, yes. But there were more men in the RPOs if we include the people from other structures in the given village. A total in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica was 6.034 plus the 1.999 members of both the active and reserve force. Therefore, the total was 8.033.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you said, this was the situation in 1998 and in early 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one, this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the manning strength.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures I mentioned or the ones we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The figures you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the RPOs come the beginning of the war? What happened with the people who were within the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had their war assignments were deployed to the units; those who did not remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you assist us in the following: Which units could these people have had war assignments in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the military territorial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would these be the civilian protection, the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the civilian protection, according to the Geneva Conventions, were unarmed. However, the units of the civil defence carried light weapons, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And some had?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had their war assignments with the VJ, because the VJ also comprised its peacetime nucleus and the reserve force. Once a mobilisation is carried out so as to bring up to strength the VJ units according to the establishment, they had to draw on the reserve force as well, unless we are discussing the A-type units which are fully manned in peacetime as well. If these units were the B-type units, they drew from the reserves. It all depended on the given unit, its place and role within the plan of use of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Yesterday we mentioned the village of Bukos. At page 9 of this document in the B/C/S under number 12 we find -- just a moment until we have that on the screen. In item 12 there is a reserve police squad in the village of Bukos.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This RPO comprised a total of six members. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, I've noted yesterday that the figures you were giving were actually for March 1999, following the reduction of forces after the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the data I specified now refer to 1998. In the whole of territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, there were 14.576 policemen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 14.571 policemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement was signed, there was a reduction down to 10.021. That was the situation until the beginning of March 1999. At that time there was a mobilisation which brought the figure back to 14.571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that the starting figure for the complement of regular police including PJP in Kosovska Mitrovica of 1.999 applied in October rather than in March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you gave us a figure for the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figure I mentioned was 1999 in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998. That figure, once the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement was signed, was reduced by 600 in Kosovska Mitrovica itself. Then in March the figure was back to the old number, 1.999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. I have noted yesterday that that figure of 1.999 applied as of the declaration of an imminent state of war on the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the figure of 6.034 for the reserve police squads and other groupings of men, does that figure relate to March 1999 as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Out of those 6.034, some of those men went off to other units where they had their war assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, now we are going to look at the next page on e-court, numbers 14, 15, and 16. We're talking about the municipality of Vucitrn. I'm going to ask you about the police squads of Samodreza; that's under number 14. It has five members. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under number 15, the Mijalic reserve police had five?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the reserve police department of Miroce has four members. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that all of these villages are in the municipality of Vucitrn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that the population of these villages could not defend themselves from the KLA and never mind going into any kind of action?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about weaponry and a light machine-gun. Because this is a domestically made weapon, people don't know what it looks like. Is it true that the machine-gun is the same as an automatic rifle, it uses the same kind of ammunition, of the same calibre, but only has a tripod where you can rest it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on which one it is, an E-53 or M-72.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you this, and this is a question that His Honour Judge Bonomy was also interested in at page 1222, and that was did the police reserve units receive any specific assignments from the SUPs, for example, or were they just guarding villages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly meant for the defence of villages. They were defending and guarding the villages. That was their purpose. In a certain zone, however, where these RPOs were and units of the Army of Yugoslavia were engaged or the PJPs in carrying out certain assignments, then the commanders of those units could engage those units for assignments in that particular sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. With the declaration of the state of war, the organisation of the defence is completely different. They are now headed by a staff, at whose head is the president of the municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which staffs you are thinking of and which plans. In the defence system, there are other plans. Are you thinking of plans of defence of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It would be the municipal operative staffs or whatever they are called.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have one more thing here. No, no, it's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P1115 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with this document but with the previous one. Do you know if members of the RPOs at the beginning of the war, those who did not go to their units in accordance with their war assignment, at that time after the 24th of March, 1999, did they have full uniforms, insignia, and all of that. You said they didn't have that in 1998. Did everybody have them in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you definitely. Some did and some didn't. But they did [Realtime transcript read in error "didn't"] have their basic military or soldier's insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I apologise for losing time, and I'm actually trying to cut my cross-examination short.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P1968 on the e-court monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already talked about this order with my colleagues. At the top it states "Joint Command for KiM." If you would look at this document more closely, and you can do that if you wish, but I am actually telling you that the police are not instructed to do anything in this document. The police units are not cited, police assignments are not referred to, and you yourself said that this was a military document. Is it then a Joint Command at some military level or a Joint Command that was supposed to unify the activities of the army and the police or some third kind of Joint Command, but is it correct that in this document the police is not referred to in the sense that I mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to look at the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me look at the heading of the document first, please. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll up, please, up. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the heading it says: "Joint Command for KiM." It does not say: "Joint Military Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but if you need to you will have time to read through the whole document and then you will see that units and tasks and locations of the police are not mentioned in this document. All that is mentioned are the units, tasks, and locations of the military units.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it's a question of perhaps the police already being at those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, the Pristina Corps is being issued an assignment. It also refers to neighbours, but it doesn't say anywhere that ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I look at the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3 so that the witness can see it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in order to get a real proper answer we need to see whether the MUP staff didn't receive a similar order or command for the actions of its units in this section -- sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see this document before, the one that we're discussing now, which relates to your zone, Drenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I look at the first page, please? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The meeting that you attended was held on the 4th of April, 1999, at the ministry headquarters. On the first page we also see your name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page. Mr. Stamp put questions to you about this document. On page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3, please. I'm sorry, it's page 4 actually. Can we zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will see the seventh asterisk from the top. It says Obrad Stevanovic speaks, deputy minister. And it says: "The command and control of units in the area of a secretariat is done by the chiefs."

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what Mr. Stevanovic is saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which units did he mean? Can you tell us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain the terms "command and control." First of all, there was no need for that. You could only use control because control implies command. When you say "command," that implies planning and organising and commanding and coordination in joint actions and control of the function. There is no control without all of those links in the chain. If one of them is missing, you don't have any control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the chiefs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs were not in a command position, they didn't command the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move on now, please. Sometimes we say that something is not correct, but what we actually would like is for you to confirm it. So now we're going to move to the next document. Just one moment, please. I would like to ask you about civilians. Is it correct that a few days before the aggression - and especially during the first days of the war - it was evident that people were leaving Kosovska Mitrovica out of fear of the actual conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but not only because they were afraid of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People, first of all, were leaving because they were afraid of the NATO pact, because of the bombing; second, they were leaving not only Kosovska Mitrovica. The situation was the same in the entire Kosovo territory. When larger police or military forces would appear, the population would leave their places of residence. Citizens were also leaving their places of residence under the pressure of the KLA. If offensive actions were being undertaken by the military and the police in order for the KLA members to pull out of that area, they would use the population to pull out. There were also individuals who -- who would enter apartments and houses and who were actually forcing the population to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing about this. Is it correct that you didn't know that there was a policy and a plan according to which people were supposed to be transferred from a specific area to another area or were to be expelled?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You mean did a plan exist like a plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was no such plan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such a plan as a plan did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a good time for a break and we could maybe go through our questions and see maybe we won't have too many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Just a couple of matters, though, arising out of what you've just said, Mr. Cvetic. When you say there were people who entered apartments and houses, actually forcing the population to leave their homes, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were policemen, members of the reserve force, and of the RPO. It depended on the situation and where it took place. Otherwise, these were individual cases. It was only in the initial stage of the aggression, at this critical moment when bombs started falling until the situation was stabilised. The critical period was approximately between the 24th of March until late March or up to the 4th of April when the situation began stabilising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My second question relates to the situation you describe where larger police or military forces appeared and you tried to explain what the KLA did. Now, I didn't follow how that affected the population. Could you explain that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The population left their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica, there was a lot -- well, in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica, between the 24th of March and until the 16th of April, there were 90 people killed, the bodies of whom we found and we registered those cases. They were murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But what I'm trying to establish is what the relationship between the appearance of larger forces of police and military was and people leaving. What was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an exchange of fire between the KLA and the army and the police on the other side, and then people would abandon that area. However, the population tended to leave the area as soon as a larger number of troops of the military and the police would appear, because they presumed what might ensue would be a conflict in exchange of fire or a skirmish. And then they left the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall break again. Could you please go with the usher, and we'll be resuming again in this instance at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have only one administrative matter and I wanted the witness to be present. In the transcript, page 60, line 14, it is entered "didn't" and should be entered "did." And the witness was talking about reserve police detachments, that they did have basic uniforms and insignia, and in the transcript it says "didn't." So if necessary, it can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I agree that that's what -- well, sorry, perhaps you should ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, these things happen sometimes. Sometimes things are not quite correctly recorded in the transcript. Did you say that in 1999 members of reserve police sections, who were not engaged in their wartime units, had their military uniform and insignia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only military, they had their police uniforms and insignia, their basic insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted corrected, they did. You spoke and Judge Bonomy asked you about the criminal conduct of individuals. Is it the case that those were really individuals, as you said, criminals, and that there was several orders to intervene, to apprehend them, to detain them, and punish them, the people who entered homes, looted, robbed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing. You were speaking about the 17th of March, 1999, about the meeting when the head of staff, Sreten Lukic, made mention of volunteers. Do you remember who else attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of March? All chiefs of secretariats from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was a regular meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was a regular meeting of the staff of the MUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked you about unofficially armed persons. He actually meant paramilitaries; namely, the group that was active on the Kosovska Mitrovica-Ribarice road.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said those people were expelled from your area and you never saw them again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did those people enter the territory of Kosovo somewhere from Serbia or Montenegro and operated in the border area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that area -- was that area close to the border with Serbia or Montenegro or both?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvetic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Cvetic, my name is Aleksander Aleksic, attorney-at-law. I have just a few questions for you. You told us that from 1990 to 1996 you were head of the SUP of Kragujevac. Can you tell me about the period before that. What was your occupation, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want my entire career or just the period immediately before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, just from 1982 until 1990.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was head of SUP in Kragujevac -- I was head of the SNO in Kragujevac, secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So you were secretary of the secretariat for national defence for eight years?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Six years. In connection with that, I wanted to ask you something about the system of territorial defence, if you have knowledge about that. Would I be right in saying that the system of territorial defence was organised at the republic and provincial level?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What system are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Territorial defence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: From 1982 to 1990, when you were in that position.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO system was organised at the republic and province levels. There was a republic TO staff and the province TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that the arming and equipping of TO units was the responsibility of the republics and provinces of the then-SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the republics and provinces were owners of the entire assets, both materiel and the weaponry, that belonged to TO units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to distinguish between various TO units, whether they belonged to the manoeuvreing structure or the zonal structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'll move to something else. I wanted to ask you in this connection, would I be right in saying that the republic staff and the province staffs of the TO were subordinated to civilian authorities, unlike the system of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question on this topic. After the break-up of the SFRY, did the TO system collapse as well and was replaced by another system?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that after the dissolution of that system which resulted from the dissolution of the state, the new resulting states became owners of the -- those weapons and equipment that existed at the local republic level?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we have to distinguish between manoeuvreing units and zonal units because some TO units did hand over, return, their weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But the part of it was retained?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this. During examination-in-chief, and in cross-examination as well, your evidence was that you did not attend a single meeting of the Joint Command, you did not take part in any anti-terrorist actions in 1999, and you didn't see the document that was shown you yesterday and today relating to your territory and concerning the conduct of anti-terrorist actions. My question is: How then do you know that the Joint Command adopted and verified plans?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what is written in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But at the time when this document was generated, you said that you did not see it in responding to a question by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one, but I saw similar documents with the same heading, with the same signature of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. During examination-in-chief yesterday, you said that the Joint Command was set up to coordinate activities between the army and the police in view of anti-terrorist actions that took place between the 25th of July and the 29th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was set up just before the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But those anti-terrorist operations were conducted between the 25th of July and the 29th of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple quick questions, I hope. You said that the MUP staff meetings were held in the Grand Hotel. Where was this Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that members of the Joint Command included one Mr. Matkovic and another Mr. Minic, and you were asked questions about who -- about seniority, I think. Can I just ask you one thing. Can you recall the period when these persons -- well, let's take them one by one. Can you recall the period when Mr. Matkovic was a member of the Joint Command; in particular, was he a member after November of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After November, I did not see Mr. Matkovic on the territory covered by Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, but I saw him in the beginning of July 1998. And he was at a meeting that was held in the offices of the director of the Trepca mining complex to deal with problems in the functioning of one system within the mining complex, which was a bit further removed from Trepca itself. It was under the control of a terrorist group. The process of control was made very difficult, and the question was how to deal with it. And he was at that meeting. But after November, I didn't see him; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow your answer. Do you know whether or not he remained a member of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting at the staff of MUP of Pristina held on the 5th of November, 1998, that meeting was also attended by the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic. And, among other things, he reported then that the Joint Command would remain in the same composition as when it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, if you let me say just one more thing, there was also the minister of the interior, who introduced Mr. Radomir Markovic, the new chief of the administration of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was it said that the Joint Command would remain in the same composition as when it was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from that, did Mr. Milutinovic play any other role at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milutinovic had a prior meeting with political and business figures and leaders of Kosovo and Metohija. And after that meeting, he attended the meeting attended by all chiefs of secretariats, commanders of units, and heads of the departments of internal affairs and the State Security Service. On that occasion, Mr. Milutinovic spoke about Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement which had 11 points, and he gave a detailed explanation of each of the 11 points. On that occasion he also said that the OSCE mission had representatives from 53 countries, that there were 2.000 monitors in Kosovo, and that those monitors had to be given everything that we have so that they can gain an insight into the real state of affairs. That was the gist of his contribution. He spoke, of course, about political and economic issues, saying that the Republic of Serbia would invest maximum efforts to help Kosovo and to help the situation in Kosovo to be dealt with peacefully, using political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say if Mr. Milutinovic attended any -- or let me put it this way. Was this the only meeting of the MUP staff that you attended in which Mr. Milutinovic was present or were there others?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. On the 23rd September, Mr. Milutinovic attended the same kind of meeting with approximately the same attendees, including chiefs of secretariats, all chiefs of secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his role there or how did he participate in that meeting, if at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that occasion he said that terrorism in Kosovo was defeated, terrorist groups were destroyed, and that all the necessary premises had been created for the problems in Kosovo to be resolved by peaceful means. Only small, minor terrorist groups remained that did not constitute a major security problem, that all the premises existed for the security situation to improve, and that everybody will work in their line of work to help resolve the problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, was Mr. Lukic present at either of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could get back to what I was asking before. I take it from your answers that you are not quite sure about the period when Mr. Matkovic was a member of the Joint Command. Is that understanding correct? In which case we could move on to Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I emphasised that Mr. Matkovic was there in July, that I saw him personally. I didn't see him after November. But Mr. Milutinovic at that meeting of the 5th of November said that the Joint Command would remain in the same composition as when it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were shown Exhibit P1044 and I'd like to show it to you again. And it was suggested to you that the MUP of Serbia could and would inform and give directions to the SUPs without referring to the MUP staff Pristina.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll get to the question --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the MUP in Pristina or the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The MUP staff. I'm getting to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at section 2 of that document; that is on page 3 of the English version and page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see at paragraph 5 it is indicated that the secretariats of the interior in Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica, Urosevac, Gnjilane, Djakovica, Pec, and Prizren sent dispatches both to the ministry and to the ministry staff in Pristina. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to the last page, and that is the item numbered 5 on the last page. In -- it says there: "When an organisational unit from the ministry main office sends dispatches, it addresses them as follows: (1) SUP to all 1 to 33 staff of the ministry Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So having regard to that and your own knowledge of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe translation mistake but here it says under 5, in B/C/S at least: "In one of following ways." "In one of following ways." [Interpretation] "In one of the following ways." [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... all of them, at least according to B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cvetic, could you read the first two lines of the paragraph number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When an organisational unit from the main office of the ministry sends dispatches, it shall be addressed in one of the following ways." I don't understand what this means. "When an organisational unit from the base of the ministry," and then no see any more text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness cannot see the whole text; that's why he is confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It needs to be moved a little. "It shall address them in one of the following ways." First: "SUP to all 1 to 33 ministry staff Pristina. "2: SUP in (indicate name of secretariat). "3. SM to border control post to all. "4. SM to border control post (indicate name of the police station)." Yes this is written here. It's dated 25th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now having regard to that particular item 1 of section 5 which you just read, that one of the ways in which a dispatch could be sent is to all the SUPs and staff of the ministry in Pristina, and also the previous item indicating that the secretariats for the -- for Kosovo and Metohija should send both to the ministry and the ministry staff in Pristina, and having regard to your own knowledge of what the practice was while you were there when dispatches and reports were sent by the SUP staff, would the ministry staff in Pristina, that is the Pristina staff, also be copied?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on what is contained in the dispatch received by the secretariat. If the secretariat received a dispatch from one of the police administrations of the MUP on which they had to act and if it is stated inside the dispatch that they are responsible directly to the administration sending out the dispatch, then it was so. This example concerns an aggravated theft and a pursuit of a fugitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I put the question this way then: In dispatches or reports sent by the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija to the ministry relating to -- that is the ministry in Belgrade, relating to combat manoeuvres in Kosovo and Metohija, would the ministry staff in Pristina normally be copied on those dispatches and reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, there is the sign of equation between the term "dispatch" and the term "daily report." The difference is great, though. As for daily reports on current events interesting for security matters in the past 24 hours, such reports were supposed to be sent by the SUPs to the staff in Pristina and the duty office. They were only duty-bound to respond to a dispatch by way of communicating directly with the organ which sent the dispatch in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that answers the other part of the question. In the case of a dispatch sent by a SUP in Kosovo to the ministry in Belgrade relating to combat manoeuvres in Kosovo, would the ministry staff in Pristina normally be copied that dispatch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be a regular occurrence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when the various units of the MUP were engaged in operations in the field, the procedure for controlling them and commanding them would be different. Can you explain that? When the various units of the MUP were engaged in operations in Kosovo, how were they commanded and what part did the MUP staff for Pristina have in respect to those engagements?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP staff forwarded orders to unit commanders, to the commanders of those units participating in certain operations. Such unit commanders directly commanded their units and reported to the MUP staff on the activities undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- you said that the chain of command of both the MUP organisation and the VJ did not change after the Joint Command had been established, and further you said that the SUP chiefs were not duty-bound to report to the Joint Command. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prescribed by the law, and the command responsibility is defined in both military and police. The Joint Command was formed to coordinate activities between the army and the police and to verify and approve certain plans which involved both the units of the police and the army. But the chain of command in place was following the law, strictly speaking. That's why the chiefs of secretariats did not inform the command, but chiefs of secretariats informed the member of the MUP staff who was included in the joint chain of command. The Joint Command was not an extraordinary body in the sense that it existed outside the system that was in place for the army and the police. In the Joint Command, one could find the most responsible people from the police and the army in the area of Kosovo, that is Messrs. Pavkovic and Lukic. They were at the Joint Command, they were part of it, members of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You say that the MUP staff in Kosovo received information - I think you used the word "exclusively" - from the MUP organs in Kosovo, but from -- also from its own staff members. I'll get to the question in a moment, in a moment, Mr. Cvetic, I'm just trying to find precisely what you said. Right. You said the MUP staff in Kosovo did not have its own personnel to collect information -- withdrawn. I'll quote you directly. You said the MUP staff in Kosovo received information exclusively from the SUPs but also from its own staff members who were tasked in specific areas as part of their staff work. Do you know if the MUP staff in Kosovo would have received information also from the manoeuvre or combat units in the field?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There was the obligation of those units to inform the head of the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also said that each of the assistants to the chief of the MUP staff had specific areas of responsibility. Can you remember generally what these areas of responsibility were, if you could remember the various assignments of the assistants to the MUP Pristina chief?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the MUP staff in Pristina had his assistants for specific spheres of work. For example, for the police he had one assistant; for crime, he had another; and he had people from -- for general crime and for serious crime. For interventions, there was another assistant. For security, another person. For the mechanised units, yet another, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, for security, what was the security department about? What was the role of the security department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What department?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the role of the security department or the -- what was the role of the person responsible for security affairs in the ministry staff Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security assistant with the staff did not exist as far as I know. There were 14 people headed by the Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... problem. "Obezbedjenje," "bezbednost". The witness said "obezbedjenje," and it was probably translated into English to "bezbednost," and when it was translated back that's why there is a confusion now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer we're concerned about is line 1 on page 80?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, the word that was used at that stage should have been translated in what do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's hard. In English can be translated both terms with one word, but in Serbian it means completely different "obezbedjenje" means something like a guard; and "bezbednost" means security. So guard and protection is "obezbedjenje," as I understand, so that's -- that's-- maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're concerned about "bezbednost," I think, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is no such thing; that's why the witness is confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll get the thing precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there an assistant responsible for information gathering -- intelligence and information gathering?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean an analyst?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Something is wrong with the -- no, not an analyst. Gathering information from the field of operation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that person was not in charge of security. He was an analyst or an administrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the role of this analyst or administrator in respect to gathering information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To gather information, to process them, and forward them to the ministry, and to the chief of the staff. If that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on from there. You said that the -- the police personnel had been -- by March you had 14.571 police personnel present in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you manage to muster this number before or after the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear about this figure because that's not my note. I've noted the figure of 14.571 as being the figure before reduction following the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. The figure then went down to 10.021, and yesterday the witness said that by the 20th of March it had risen again to between 14.500 and 15.000. Now, I know that 14.571 falls into that range, but to avoid confusion let me check whether what I just said is the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can't get into the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14.571, that was the number of police officers in Kosovo before the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. Once it was signed, what remained was 10.021. Once a mobilisation was proclaimed in March, the figure went up again to between 14.500 and 15.000. However, the figure of 14.571 existed at the time of signing and that's the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the M-53 light machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an infantry weapon, an infantry weapon that uses 7.9-millimetre ammunition. This is the M-53. The M-72 uses 7.62-millimetre ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cvetic, that completes your evidence to the Tribunal. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You are now free to leave us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who will be the next witness, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness would be Mr. Sterenberg, who is scheduled for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And he's scheduled to -- yeah, so you've got him scheduled for two hours on Monday. Then what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness -- we're going to have a problem. I should advise the Court. We are trying to get back-up witnesses, and we have done, I think, everything possible, and we are still trying to get some back-up witnesses. The problem being that the -- shall I say the relatively uncomplicated witnesses, most of them have already testified and almost anybody that can be identified now would present a problem for the Defence. But there will be problems next week which the Prosecution will encounter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, speaking for myself, I'm not readily persuaded that with a witness list the length of your witness list it should be impossible to arrange matters so that there is some evidence to fill next week, which was a week we specifically provided for slightly extended hours and gave notice, I think, three weeks or more ago about that. So I hope that these efforts continue and that the position improves, because I think there is only one other witness provided in your list for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For sure. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you want us to change arrangements for him as well, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it would be convenient to bring him forward, convenient not just to him but to -- also to the Court since there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the informal information I have is that he wouldn't be arriving here until midday on Wednesday. Is that -- has that changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you going to try to change it though?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We -- we will try to change it. We will try to bring some witness to fill the time that is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you see, on Wednesday we are programmed to sit from 9.00 until 3.30. Now, we won't get much of his evidence on Wednesday if that arrangement remains in place. So do you wish us to change that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you have a proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, the answer to the question is that we've done everything we could to try to bring him earlier and he cannot be here before noon on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But you anticipate that he'll go straight into giving evidence when he arrives? This is not a witness who has to be proofed or delayed in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was one of the witnesses that we managed to proof earlier, before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is 12.00 the time for his arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think he arrives in the country at 12.00, and we will make efforts to bring him straight to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I suppose if that remains the situation, we would be willing to sit in the afternoon on Wednesday instead of the morning, but it would be very helpful if he could arrive earlier and we could get the same length of sitting but adjust the time of it. He's not coming from very far away, is he? Or is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, he's coming from -- I understand not from his home country but from some distance away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'd be grateful if counsel would have in mind the possibility that on Wednesday the sitting time might go back to the afternoon, finishing at 7.00. But hopefully we'll have a clearer picture of when it is anticipated he can get to the Tribunal, either on Monday or Tuesday, to make the appropriate announcement -- in fact, it will have to be Monday the way things stand at the moment if you don't have another witness to fill in on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we shall now adjourn until Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
